Enjoying this newsletter? Get it in your inbox every weekend, as well as our daily round-up of The Economist’s best journalism, by signing up for free here. A number of are allowing couples having children via IVF to assess embryos based on their genetic risk of diseases such as breast cancer and diabetes. Some venture further into science-fiction territory, providing scores for IQ and height, or even eye and hair colour. Critics level that fertility entrepreneurs could be this century’s eugenicists. Our leader argues there is an important difference. The world’s biggest fast-food chain is not McDonald’s; it’s not even American. Until now it has made money from bubble tea and ice cream. Soon its servers will be pulling pints, too. Bo Franklin, Senior digital editor What to expect in the week ahead: ▸Japan has just published GDP data. The country’s economy grew by 1.1% on an annualised basis in the second quarter—considerably below analysts’ expectations of 2%. High energy prices caused by the Iran war, weak consumer spending and low investment all contributed to the disappointing figures, though the slow growth was partially offset by strong export figures. ▸ Investors will get a snapshot of how American consumers are feeling this week, as Walmart, Target and Home Depot report earnings. When consumers are stressed about the economy, spending on household goods and clothes are among the first things they shelve. America’s war with Iran has pushed up prices, especially of petrol, hurting the wallets of even prosperous consumers. ▸ On Tuesday Floridians will vote in the state’s primary gubernatorial elections. Voters will decide which Democrat and Republican will battle to become governor in November. Byron Donalds, a Republican congressman, is expected to win his party’s nomination handily, and polls predict he’ll become governor. Florida was once a quintessential swing state—but it has become a bastion of Republican power.
